posts.author: SpritesOnInstinct
posts.body: With how I am making this game I am worried I will run into over 999 maps.  Is there anyway I could tell the engine that it turns out that I need say 1300 instead for instance someone gave me a real good answer at one time but i lost the answer. Anything would be appreciated.

posts.author: VideoWizard
posts.body: The limit is 2000 maps, not 999, since they changed it in an update. But yes, that would be useful in the next maker or a 1.9.0 update, just tell the engine what the maximum number of maps you want to use is, default being, say, 2000 or up it to 5000.

posts.author: JohnDoeGames
posts.body:
I'm just going to be blunt here. Please don't take it personal.
In all those years, I've seen many developers with huge dreams and ambitions. They ask for more maps, more common events, more items... But in the end, I never actually saw a game, that indeed did have many hundreds of maps. And when I do see a game with many maps, those maps are large, empty and boring. A good map isn't made in 12 minutes, you can't make 16 good maps a day...
I am not trying to take a dump on your dreams... But with realistic goals there is an actual chance you'll succeed.
And, sorry, but I don't believe in 999 or 1300 quality maps. That would take you
a couple of years
to just draw the maps, not even including any of the programming.
This is an example of how I see many, many maps made quickly and plenty:
(Map was made by me as example)
It might have no need for anything else but a path and a house, but it is ugly and boring. If you have 999 maps looking like this, than you may as well make 0 maps, because no-one is interested in playing this.
I am not even joking... I actually see people asking for feedbacks, who ONLY have maps looking like this. And those are not even the worst maps I've ever seen.
Here is another map:
This map (also by me) might not have much to interact with either, but there is plenty to see. Everything in this map is carfuly placed, so it will make sense, so it will look natural and so it directs the player when I want them to go.
The difference is that the first map was created in a minute, while the second map took me 2 days to complete or something.
And even if you're twice as fast as me, than you'd make 1 map a day. It would still take 3 years to draw 999 maps that way.
If you really, really want 999+ maps in your game, then of course that is your right, but I'll say it again: Quality over quantity any time.

posts.author: redtide89
posts.body:
Okay but there are many reasons to use additional maps.
Some of my maps are copies of another map.
About 65% of them are playable/explorable, the other 35% are used for other purposes, like story, cutscenes, or just making my work easier even if it's sloppy or bad practice. I'm not here to say how things should be done, just that they could be done this way.
Like my biggest map which is 179x100 tiles is actually just sixteen evenly-spaced interiors of a single village. The village itself is a medium-size map (for my game), and each interior is tiny. Some have a second floor, some have a basement, some have a before/after version, and each one takes a different interior map so I consolidated them into one map thinking this would be a good idea. It was probably not a good idea and I haven't done it since. All I'm saying is that this single village has only two maps -- an exterior and an interior. If I did it today, it would be made with probably seventeen maps (an exterior and sixteen individual tiny interiors).
The vast majority of my cutscenes occur on playable maps that can have npcs walking around and doing whatever they do (talking to each other, fake text boxes appearing with their dialogue, etc), and I just have to keep that in mind when making them. Some of my cutscenes occur on maps made exclusively for the story and are not explorable/playable beyond this. In both cases, there is only one rpg maker map for each game map.
However, for some maps/cutscenes it's easier to just copy the entire map and use the duplicate for a story segment or something, especially if I need to do something weird that might interfere with events or npcs on the main/playable version of the map.
Sometimes it's just laziness. Like I have a small map that is just a hallway with a door in the center, blocking your path. You can open it, sort of, but rather than taking the time to draw and animate the door opening, I just made a second version of the map that has the door already open. So if the door is "open", the player transfers to the open hallway version, and if it's closed (blocked/locked) it goes to the closed hallway version. This is super lazy, but I didn't feel like putting in the effort at the time since I'd like to finish the meat of the game and not work on tiny details like this right now. In the future I might just remove one of the hallway maps, and have a functioning, openable door in the middle of the hallway that looks good to me. As it is right now, if I absolutely have to, interacting with the door to open it can just teleport the player to the open hallway map and although it is a little jank, with even a little bit of effort you can hide the fact that it is happening and the player is none the wiser.
To make matters worse, if you implemented a system for your game that sort of necessitates a second version of nearly every playable map, things could get out of hand very quickly and you might reach that 999+ maps sooner than you think.
For example, if your game was set up to let the player press a button to activate a 'dream' state where the map changed slightly (like a few purple filters thrown everywhere, every npc changes graphics/dialogue/etc, different stuff floating around the screen, maybe a dark/nighttime aesthetic applied to the base map), and the way you went about this is just sort of using a second version of each map to have the dream version of that map accessible to the player. This might be a reasonable way to do this. Are there different ways? Yes, of course. Are there better ways? Probably so. Does this work? Probably. But it would nearly double the number of maps your game needs despite not being anywhere close to doubling the work you'd need to do.
Also, I have about 30 or so test maps that are just not in use but aren't really needed for the game that I'm not counting. If I remake a map I'll usually just move the old one up to my test maps folder instead of deleting it. Sometimes I'll use them to test stuff out on or experiment with new ideas instead of making yet another map to try this out on (or testing stuff out in a different project entirely).
Anyway, what I'm getting at is for someone like me, my game is pretty normal and I don't think 130 maps is too many or too few. It seems perfectly reasonable, but my project has like 160ish due to unused maps. I'd guess that about 10-15% of the playable maps are duplicates for story purposes or mechanical laziness on my part rather than necessity, but for me, additional maps take far less time/space/resources than making specific animations, additional graphics/backgrouns/parallax layers/etc to achieve almost the same effect. Someone else using these techniques might take them much farther than I have, and end up with hundreds of maps very easily and surprisingly quickly, even with having a fully-fledged quality game underneath it all.
EDIT: Quality is still more important than quantity, but I think that it's possible to generate quality for the game in different ways -- one of which being simply making use of extra maps to achieve a high-quality, desired result that could also be achieved with similar but possibly greater effort inside of a single map.

posts.author: utunnels
posts.body: I wonder why there's even a limit in the first place. They could just be lazy and did not add the hard limit, and let the user complain about their editors frozen because they have 12345 maps.

posts.author: Zeriab
posts.body:
utunnels said:
I wonder why there's even a limit in the first place. They could just be lazy and did not add the hard limit, and let the user complain about their editors frozen because they have 12345 maps.
Click to expand...
Precisely this, or so I believe. MZ gets noticeable sluggish when you are above 1500+ maps. Only raising the map limit to 2000 is cheaper than spending time optimizing the editor.
Once you play the game itself there's no performance issue. Here you would be able to easily have 100k maps.
When talking about performance it's worth mentioning that compiling several maps into one, is a form of deoptimization given how RPG Maker work. Beyond the performance hit, you may also encounter bugs caused by events coming from one map interferring with events coming from another map.
